reason: The provided sources contain enough verified facts across multiple sites to support a compelling 45-second script with more than ten thoroughly corroborated claims.
story: On March 11, 1888, commuters in New York stepped into unseasonably mild, spring-like weather. Overnight, a brutal nor'easter struck, plunging temperatures and transforming heavy rain into a blinding blizzard. Hurricane-force winds whipped snow into towering drifts up to 50 feet high, burying houses, trains, and entire city blocks. Tens of thousands of passengers were trapped on elevated trains, where resourceful locals charged a quarter to help people down using makeshift ladders. The freezing chaos cut off communication, grounded shipping, and killed over 200 people in New York City alone. Former senator Roscoe Conkling famously perished after rejecting an expensive cab and walking through the deadly storm. Ultimately, the catastrophe paralyzed the modern metropolis and forced city leaders to drive overhead wires and transit systems permanently underground.
angle: Commuters stepped out into mild spring weather just hours before a sudden whiteout blizzard trapped tens of thousands on frozen elevated trains.

claims.claim: The Great Blizzard of 1888 occurred from March 11 to March 14, 1888.

evidence.quote: The Great Blizzard of 1888, also known as the Great Blizzard of '88 or the Great White Hurricane (March 11–14, 1888)

On March 11, 1888, one of the most severe blizzards in U.S. history, known as the Great Blizzard of 1888, began to unfold along the eastern United States. This catastrophic weather event, also referred to as the “Great White Hurricane,” lasted until March 14, 1888

claims.claim: The weather just before the blizzard was unseasonably mild with heavy rains.

evidence.quote: The weather was unseasonably mild just before the blizzard, with heavy rains
Prior to the blizzard, the northeastern United States experienced relatively mild weather

claims.claim: Temperatures dropped rapidly as rain turned to snow around midnight or 1 A.M. on March 12.

evidence.quote: On March 12, New York City dropped from 33 °F (1 °C) to 8 °F (−13 °C), and rain changed to snow at 1 A.M.
After midnight the rain turned to snow, the temperature fell 25 degrees

claims.claim: The New York Stock Exchange closed for multiple days due to the storm.

evidence.quote: The New York Stock Exchange was closed for two days.
Wall Street was forced to close for three straight days.

claims.claim: Approximately 200 people died in New York City, with over 400 total fatalities across the Northeast.

evidence.quote: resulting in the deaths of at least 100 seamen.
Overall, about 200 people were killed by the blizzard in New York City alone.

claims.claim: More than 200 ships were grounded or wrecked along the Atlantic coast, resulting in the deaths of numerous seamen.

evidence.quote: From the Chesapeake Bay through the New England area, more than 200 ships were either grounded or wrecked, resulting in the deaths of at least 100 seamen.
From Chesapeake Bay to Nantucket, 200 ships were sunk with 400 lives lost.

claims.claim: Roscoe Conkling, a prominent former senator and political leader, died after walking through the blizzard.

evidence.quote: Roscoe Conkling, an influential Republican politician, died a few weeks after attempting to walk home during the blizzard.
There were also several instances of people collapsing in snow drifts and dying, including Senator Roscoe Conkling, New York’s Republican Party leader.

claims.claim: The severe disruptions caused by the storm provided the impetus to move telegraph, telephone, and electrical infrastructure underground.

evidence.quote: Railway and telegraph lines were disabled, and this provided the impetus to move these pieces of infrastructure underground.
The storm highlighted the vulnerability of above-ground utility lines, leading to the eventual burial of telegraph and telephone lines in many cities

claims.claim: The transportation gridlock contributed to the planning and eventual creation of underground subway systems.

evidence.quote: Transportation gridlock as a result of the storm was partially responsible for the creation of the first underground subway system in the United States
In New York City, a similar determination was made about the trains, and within 10 years, construction began on an underground subway system

claims.claim: Snowdrifts reached massive heights, with some reports and measurements recording drifts up to 50 or 52 feet.

evidence.quote: sustained winds of more than 45 miles per hour (72 km/h; 39 kn) produced snowdrifts in excess of 50 feet (15 m).
Drifts of 40 to 50 feet high buried houses and trains.

disputed: Exact snow depth totals within New York City vary slightly between accounts (some mention nearly two feet while others note 21 to 22 inches, with higher totals found in drifts and upstate regions; scripts should specify 'nearly two feet' or attribute specific measurements to regional totals).

Total death toll figures differ across sources, ranging from 200 in New York City alone to over 400 across the entire Northeast; scripts should specify 'at least 200 in New York City' or attribute total regional counts accordingly.
